title: Model food's path and explain absorption
subject: SCIENCE

authority.note: Original LiberiaLearn instructional draft. Academic review, standards mapping, rights review and release authorization are pending.

objectives.statement: Arrange the main stages of the digestive tract and distinguish that path from organs supplying digestive juices.
Explain absorption as digested nutrients crossing the small-intestine wall, using a counted paper model.
Use a model to explain an organ's job and identify something the model cannot show.

content.body: A fictional school group in Buchanan is preparing a poster about what happens after eating rice. Before using the poster, sketch your own idea of the route. Keep your first drawing so that you can later explain a change.

prompts.prompt: What route do you predict, and where might useful parts leave it? Label one uncertainty in your first model.

content.body: Use large paper cards and a paper food token. Move the token from mouth to anus through the route you arrange. Chewing starts breakdown; the esophagus moves food; the stomach mixes it. Digestion continues in the small intestine, where most nutrients are absorbed. The large intestine absorbs water. Its rectum stores stool before it leaves through the anus. The liver and pancreas supply juices; swallowed food does not pass through them.

scenes.title: Crossing a wall does not mean disappearing

content.body: Draw two regions: inside the small intestine, and the rest of the body. Use twelve large paper tokens for already-digested nutrients. Move five across the boundary, then five more. Keep transferred tokens in the body region. This represents absorption, not whole food leaving the stomach. The counts are invented for the model; they are not a human absorption rate.

scenes.title: Operate and check your own paper model

content.body: Use fourteen large paper tokens, drawn marks or counters too large to swallow. Mark an inside region and a body region. Move nine tokens across the wall. Keep every token visible. A crossing changes its region, not whether it exists. Starting, transferred and remaining counts describe different groups. Count both regions before answering. A partner may move tokens while you direct. Keep objects away from mouths.

prompts.prompt: Explain what one crossing models. Name one thing these paper tokens do not show about a real intestine.

scenes.title: Separate a model from evidence about a body

content.body: Compare your first route with the organ model. Explain a change using the job of an organ. The token model helps show a transfer across a wall. It does not reproduce living tissue or measure how quickly a person's body absorbs a meal.

accessibility.textAlternative: Compare your first route with the organ model. Explain a change using the job of an organ. The token model helps show a transfer across a wall. It does not reproduce living tissue or measure how quickly a person's body absorbs a meal. What does moving a nutrient token into the body region represent? Options: A digested nutrient crossing the small-intestine wall.; The nutrient ceasing to exist.; A whole mouthful passing directly from stomach to liver.. Which claim cannot be established with this paper model? Options: The original tokens can be counted across two regions.; The specified transfers leave three of sixteen tokens inside.; Every pupil absorbs a real meal in exactly two minutes..

scenes.title: Improve the Buchanan school group's poster

content.body: The fictional poster says: Food passes through the liver before reaching the stomach. The stomach absorbs all nutrients. Use the route and transfer models to replace both claims. Explain the corrections so a younger reader could follow them, while keeping the diagram's limits clear.

prompts.prompt: Correct the two poster claims using the connected route and the job of the small intestine. State one limitation. For an advanced challenge, design a clearer model that distinguishes breaking food down from absorbing the resulting nutrients, and explain how you would check its clarity.
